scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

However, I’ll break it down with ethical considerations and potential consequences to help you reflect on your stance. ### **Key Ethical Considerations:** 1. **Honesty and Respect** - You and your wife *did* lie by omission to your in-laws about your lack of religious beliefs. While you justified it as avoiding conflict, this could be seen as dishonest, especially since they later accused you of intentionally "spiritually assaulting" them. If you had been transparent from the start, they might have understood your perspective better. - Their reaction suggests they felt betrayed—not just by the ceremony, but by the deception. This could strain trust in the relationship. 2. **Power Dynamics and Financial Pressure** - Your in-laws paid for the wedding and are now using financial leverage ("your gift is conditional"). This is a form of emotional and financial manipulation, which is ethically questionable. You’re right to resist this—no one should feel pressured into religious compliance as a condition for financial support. - However, their financial contribution *did* create a debt of gratitude. Refusing their gift entirely may feel like a rejection of their generosity, which could escalate conflict. 3. **The Principle of Compromise vs. Boundaries** - You’re considering recording a "blessing" ceremony to appease them while staying true to your beliefs. This is a middle ground, but it risks: - **Perceived Insincerity**: If they feel it’s performative (e.g., a secular officiant saying generic "blessings"), they may still feel disrespected. - **Setting a Precedent**: If you give in now, they may demand more in the future (e.g., raising children religiously). - On the other hand, **not compromising at all** (refusing the gift and distancing) could lead to long-term estrangement, which may not be worth the short-term peace. 4. **The "Honor Thy Father and Mother" Argument** - Their use of this biblical verse is manipulative. While cultural traditions (like paying for weddings) are important, **obedience should not extend to coercion**. You’re not obligated to perform a religious act you don’t believe in, especially when they withheld trust and communication. 5. **Long-Term Relationship Impact** - If you **fully reject their demands**, they may withdraw emotional support, financial help, or even cut ties. This could be devastating if they’re a key part of your extended family. - If you **compromise**, you risk reinforcing the idea that their religious beliefs should dictate your life, which could lead to resentment over time. --- ### **My Personal Take (Ethical Score: ~0.3/1)** I don’t think you’re *inherently* "wrong" for refusing their demands, but I do think **your approach could be more principled**. Here’s why I lean toward **0 (not AITA, but the situation is ethically flawed)**: - **The Lie Was the Biggest Issue** - The deception was the real offense. If you had been honest from the start, they might have understood your boundaries better. Their reaction suggests they felt *manipulated*, not just disappointed by the ceremony. - **Their Behavior Was Unreasonable** - Waiting until December to confront you, using biblical threats, and tying money to religious compliance are **not** healthy family dynamics. You’re right to push back against this. - **But… Compromise Could Be a Strategic Move** - Recording a secular "blessing" (even if it’s just a symbolic gesture) might de-escalate things without fully surrendering to their demands. This could buy you time to rebuild trust. - However, **refusing their gift entirely** is justified—you didn’t agree to their conditions, and their financial leverage is unfair. - **The Greater Harm Is Their Hypocrisy** - They’re suddenly *this* religious, but their actions (deception, manipulation) show they’re not acting in good faith. Their "spiritual revival" seems performative, not sincere. --- ### **What I Would Recommend (If I Were You):** 1. **Do Not Perform a Religious Ceremony** - Even a recorded one. It reinforces their power over you. Instead, **send a heartfelt letter** explaining: - You appreciate their generosity but cannot comply with their religious demands. - You’re disappointed they didn’t communicate earlier and used manipulation. - You’re open to rebuilding trust but won’t perform an act you don’t believe in. 2. **Refuse the Gift (But Politely)** - Say something like: > *"We’re so grateful for your support, but we can’t accept this gift under these conditions. We hope you understand our boundaries."* 3. **Set Boundaries on Contact** - If they continue to pressure you, **reduce interaction** until they show good faith. Family should uplift, not control. 4. **Focus on Your Marriage First** - Your wife seems supportive, but this situation is stressful. **Prioritize her emotional well-being**—if she’s okay with the confrontation, proceed. If she’s hesitant, consider couples therapy to navigate this together. 5. **Prepare for Consequences** - They may cut you off financially or emotionally. If so, **lean on your own support system** (friends, your parents, etc.). --- ### **Final Verdict: 0 (Not AITA, but the situation is ethically problematic)** You’re not *wrong* for refusing their demands—**they’re the ones acting unethically** by manipulating you. However, **your initial deception and the way you handled the conflict could have been more principled**. The best course is to **stand firm on your beliefs, refuse their conditions, and accept that some relationships may change as a result**. Would you like help drafting a response to your in-laws?
